- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.5) over recent days, model tends to under-forecast upward moves; adjust forecast upward by 1–2% of recent mean or 0.5–1.0 price point.
- When sentiment is negative (≤ -0.5), model often over-anticipates decline; reduce forecast by 1–2% or 0.5–1.0 point to avoid “overshoot” into bearish trap.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overreacts with continued steep rise; cap forecast slope or apply mean-reversion correction to 1–2 standard deviations below peak.
- If sentiment shifts from negative to positive mid-horizon, model often fails to pivot; re-estimate forecast mid-period with upward bias aligned to sentiment reversal.
- For 30-day horizon, model underestimates true volatility in high-sentiment periods; increase forecast variance by 10–20% if sentiment > 0.7 for 5+ consecutive days.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (±0.3), model often overfits to recent trend; apply smoothing filter or use 7-day moving average to reduce noise.
- Model consistently underestimates true price in 30-day horizon when sentiment is positive and price is trending upward — add 0.5–1.0 point to forecast if sentiment > 0.7 and price > 65.00.
- If sentiment is negative and price is below 60.00, model often overcorrects downward — avoid sharp drops; cap forecast at 5–10% above recent low.
